description: Greg Dean's master writing system. Half 1 (Joke Map) manufactures setups from a topic; Half 2 (Joke Mine) manufactures punchlines for those setups using the 5 joke mechanisms. Run as a sequence: topic -> association list -> punch-premise -> setup-premise -> setups -> find connector -> name target assumption -> brainstorm reinterpretations -> write punch. Turns 'be funny' into a repeatable checklist.

exercise_name: Joke Map Step 1 — List Topics (what's wrong)
description: List subjects you personally find morally wrong or irritating and want to talk about. Prompt: 'What are some things I consider wrong that I'm interested in talking about?' These become the raw fuel for jokes, since Dean holds that comedy comes from what you think is wrong.

Pick one topic and list every concrete, specific detail related to it — identifiable particulars (specific people, objects, situations), not broad categories. Prompt: 'What are all the things I can think of that relate to my topic?' This widens the surface area for finding a target.

exercise_name: Joke Map Step 3 — Write a Punch-Premise
description: Take a detail from the association list and attach a negative opinion to it: subject + negative adjective, kept broad and general (e.g. 'Postal workers are incompetent' — NOT the over-specific 'Postal workers are incompetent at delivering mail'). A punch-premise is defined as a negative opinion about a subject; it is the attitude the eventual punchline will pay off.

exercise_name: Joke Map Step 4 — Form the Setup-Premise (reverse it)
description: Write the opposite of your punch-premise: a positive/innocent opinion about the same subject. This is the framing the audience starts in, so the joke has somewhere to fall from. (Punch-premise = negative opinion; setup-premise = its positive mirror on the same subject.)

exercise_name: Joke Map Step 5 — Write a Series of Setups
description: Generate multiple short, clear statements that express the setup-premise. Keep them simple and plain — do NOT try to be funny yet. Prompt: 'What are some examples or statements that express my setup-premise?' You now have a batch of setups ready for the Joke Mine.

exercise_name: Joke Mine — write a punchline via the 5 mechanisms
description: For a given setup: (1) find the Connector — the one word/idea in the setup that has 2+ interpretations; (2) name the Target Assumption — the obvious meaning the setup pushes you toward; (3) brainstorm a long list of alternative Reinterpretations of the connector; (4) pick the most unexpected-yet-compatible one and write it as the punch, placing the Reveal at/near the end. Repeat down a list of setups.

Take any existing joke or setup and isolate the Connector: the single thing (word, phrase, or concept) carrying at least two valid interpretations that the whole joke pivots on. Diagnostic + generative drill — Dean calls the connector 'the heart of all comedy.'

Having found the connector and named the target assumption, list as many alternative meanings of the connector as possible (other than the obvious one). The longer the list, the more punchline options; then choose the most surprising-but-compatible meaning to express. This is the core idea-generation step of the Joke Mine.

Analyze any joke by mapping its five mechanisms: what scene the audience imagines from the setup (1st Story), the Target Assumption it plants, the Connector, the Reinterpretation, and the new scene the punch creates (2nd Story). Used to diagnose why a joke didn't land and where the misdirection or reveal is weak.

Take a common idiom/expression and make it funny by using it as a setup or a punchline, or by altering a word inside it. A fill-in-the-formula generator that produces an original one-liner in minutes (from the '7 Instant Joke Writing Techniques' course).
Take a standard acronym/abbreviation (e.g. TSA, EPA) and reinvent what the letters stand for in a humorous way. Instant one-liner formula.
Invent amusing alternative names for a thing, place, or group (demonstrated with school and gay-bar examples). Instant one-liner formula.
Write a hashtag that works as a punchline, a tag, or satirical commentary on a topic. Instant one-liner formula leveraging the hashtag format.
Write an unconventional, comedic definition for a word or concept (illustrated with online dating and alcohol). Instant one-liner formula.
Invent a fake website address for comic or satirical effect. Instant one-liner formula.
Construct a humorous list (often paying off with a Rule-of-Three-style unexpected final item) using the technique framework. Instant joke formula.

exercise_name: Rule of Three / Rhythm of Three
description: Construct a three-item list where the first two items are normal, positive, same-category items that establish a pattern, and the third is an unexpected, incompatible-yet-fitting item that subverts it (e.g. 'cults: the Manson Family, Heaven's Gate, Amway'). Drill: pick a category, write two straight items, then engineer the surprising third.

exercise_name: Tag Technique 1 — tag off a new Target Assumption
description: Add an extra punchline to an existing joke without writing a new setup, by establishing a NEW target assumption that the original punch can be reinterpreted against. One of three named tag-writing techniques in Workbook 2.

exercise_name: Tag Technique 2 — tag off a new Connector
description: Add an extra punchline by finding a different connector (a different ambiguous element) in the same joke and mining a fresh reinterpretation from it — no new setup required.

exercise_name: Tag Technique 3 — tag off a new Reinterpretation
description: Add another punch by choosing a different alternative interpretation of the SAME connector (from the reinterpretation brainstorm list) and expressing it as a second punch immediately after the first. Explicitly named 'Technique 3: Tag Based on a New Target Assumption/Reinterpretation' in Workbook 2.

Editing drill: rewrite a joke's setup to the minimum words needed to plant the target assumption, cutting everything that doesn't aid the misdirection — faster, cleaner jokes that land harder. Part of Workbook 2's 'From Funny to Funnier.'

Editing drill: rewrite the punchline so the Reveal (the specific word/phrase carrying the reinterpretation) sits at the very end of the sentence, maximizing surprise and laugh. Part of Workbook 2's 'From Funny to Funnier.'

Assemble individual jokes into a routine by grouping jokes that share a premise/topic and sequencing them so each builds on the last. Named exercise ('Assembling a Routine: Routine Builder', book ch.5 / Workbook 2).

Rate each joke A/B/C (A = best), then order the set 'BCAs': open with a strong B, put the weakest C material in the middle, and close on your strongest A. Drill: take a list of jokes, rate them, re-sequence into BCA order.
Placement drill: position a weaker joke or routine between two strong ones so the laughter momentum carries it. Take a set with a weak bit and reposition it between two reliable laughs.

Write a moment late in the set that repeats (with a twist) the punchline of an earlier joke, rewarding the audience for remembering. Running gag = the same bit recurring two or more times. Drill: scan your set for an early punch worth re-triggering and engineer its reprise.

exercise_name: Act Out — turn a joke into a scene
description: Convert a told joke into a performed scene by physically and vocally embodying the people/things in it. Begin in Narrator POV to set up the scene, then drop into Self POV and/or Character POV to act it out, keeping characters inside the scene unaware of the audience (4th wall). Drill: take one joke and stage it as a mini-scene with at least two POV switches.

exercise_name: Three POVs practice rounds (Narrator / Self / Character)
description: Drill the three perceptual positions: Narrator POV (talk directly to the audience), Self POV (you, inside the scene), Character POV (someone/something else inside the scene). Practice rounds train clean transitions — change body position, eyeline, and voice for each role. Workbook 3 includes explicit POV practice rounds.

Rehearse a bit by re-living the actual experience/scene it depicts (re-imagining the moment with the three POVs) rather than memorizing the words. Dean's claim: rehearse the experience and you remember material naturally and stay authentic. Multi-phase process (preparation, enact the experience, practice performing).

Rehearse with the inner critic physically separated from the creator. Do the creative/rehearsal pass uncensored in one spot; only step to a designated 'Critic Spot' when it is time to judge and revise. Prevents 'practising self-doubt.' Workbook 3 supplies Critic Split Rehearsal Sheets to log each pass. Drill: do one full uncritiqued rehearsal pass, then move to the critic spot to note fixes.

Speak out loud, freely and emotionally, ranting about something that genuinely angers/annoys you on a given topic — without trying to be funny — to surface your authentic 'judgmental' comedic voice and raw material. The rant is then mined for premises and punchlines. Dean: that judgmental inner voice 'is the real you and that's your comedic voice.'

Interactive drill: ask an audience member a simple question ('What's your name?' / 'What do you do?'), listen to the literal answer, find the funny angle in it, then embellish and extend (riff) to discover laughs. Practiced live; relies on real responses rather than scripted lines.

Pre-write and memorize a bank of insult-jokes ('heckler lines') and quick comebacks to deploy when heckled, so you have a ready response under pressure. Drill: write and rehearse a stock of comebacks before they're needed. Covered in Workbook 4 / Handling Hecklers workshop.

Performance-prep drill: craft and rehearse a strong opening line (and avoid cliché greetings) so the set starts on a laugh. Part of Workbook 4 'Peak Performance' (preparing a show list, supplying an intro, warming up, getting on stage during the applause).

Record every performance, then review the recording to read the audience response on each joke and tailor/punch-up the script for bigger laughs. Iteration loop from Workbook 4 'Peak Performance' plus the 'Read on Material' / 'Punch Up' concepts.

Rehearsed coping routines for stage fright, pre-show jitters, going blank, and bombing, plus staying inside the 'Hurt Line' (not pushing dark material past where real pain replaces comedy). Workbook 4 'Fearless Performing' drills these recovery moves.

Group exercise: comedians pitch jokes to each other and collaboratively refine them, getting feedback on setups and punches. Featured as the 'Writing Group' lecture in the Introduction course; mirrors his live classes' feedback rounds.

Practice the mechanics of handling the mic and stand (do's and don'ts) so technique never distracts from the jokes. Short dedicated module in the book (ch.8), Workbook material, and the Introduction course.
